messages.author: 052043ccfb2b3d1c
messages.subject: Inference from ferry data
parts:
I am currently analysing a data set primarily collected on ferry routes.
In some areas, there are multiple routes through a wider area giving
fairly good spatial coverage - so I plan to analyse this using the DSM
engine.=20

=20

However, in other areas, there are data from multiple years on a single
route in a big "sea area". The idea is to generate density estimates
along the route for comparisons between years. I have my project set up
with year as the stratum. As the number of samplers is restricted
(transect sampled on the outward and return in any one trip), I want to
restrict my inferences only to the surveyed area. I've referred to the
Distance help and see that the main effect of this type of set up is on
the variance of the density estimate and that you should remove the
component of variance due to the variability in encounter rate between
samplers by setting the over-dispersion parameter to zero.=20

=20

I'm not confident I've got this set up right. Within a year (stratum),
there are multiple trips - line transects (2 line transects per trip ,
albeit more or less the same, on the outward and return) - there is a
lot of variability in the encounter rate between trips. How is this
represented in the approach above?=20

=20

Sorry if this is a stupid question!=20

=20

Many thanks

Kelly=20


--

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Inference from ferry data
parts:
Kelly:

Not a stupid question. Your suggestion for the 'other areas' where
there is just a single route (transect) within an area is to do
design-based (CDS) density estimation.

If you wish to restrict your inference only to the region covered by the
effort exerted in that single transect then under these circumstances
(and these circumstances alone, for other readers of the list hoping to
justify the use of single transect survey designs) you would enter the
transits of the ferry route separately.

This is not the type of survey design to try at home, and you realise
the weaknesses of this analysis. If the animals in your population of
interest were to move just slightly so as to be outside the covered
region from one year to the next, you could conclude that there had been
a massive change in the population when instead the change had been only
down to slight spatial re-assortment. That is why we bang on ad nauseum
on this list about having adequate spatial replication in design-based
surveys.

messages.author: e87c178e8547c106
messages.subject: Re: Inference from ferry data
parts:
Hi Kelly, list:

Any variance is the answer to a question, "how would my answer change if I
carried out a set of replicate surveys according to specified rules?"
It's the "rules" for generating the replicate surveys that determine how
you estimate the variance, and how you interpret the estimated variance
when you've got it.

In your case, you have an estimate of density, Dhat, restricted to a
single search strip, from a sample of k replicates in time (but no
replicates in space). You want to estimate var(Dhat). The variance
needs to be understood as the variance over time, instead of the usual
variance over space. It expresses how your Dhat estimate would change if
you repeatedly carried out replicate surveys, where each replicate survey
consisted of a different k points in time.

It seems to me that the usual theory applies, i.e. you do include the
encounter rate variance to get a within-year estimate of var(Dhat) from
your k trips. But there are some points to consider:

1. Does every trip cover the same line length? If so this simplifies
things, because the encounter rate variance reduces to the variance of a
sample mean: you don't have to consider how line length would change in
your "replicate surveys". Then encounter rate variance is

var(nbar / l) = var(nbar) / l^2,

where l is the line length on a single trip (constant), and nbar is the
sample mean of the number of detections per trip. So it just means
finding the variance of the sample mean, which is (often) easy. But leads
to the following question:

2. Do your k trips constitute a random sample over time? i.e. is any
trip, on any day of the year, exposed to the same spectrum of encounter
possibilities as any other trip? If so - everything is easy: the usual
Distance encounter rate variance estimates should be fine. Examples where
this might not be so easy are:

- Seasonality: are the animals present at higher density at some times of
year? If so, how are the trip times aligned with the seasonal patterns in
density? The sort of situation where this might cause problems is when
animal density is highest in summer and trips are also more frequent in
summer. (This would be a problem for your estimate of Dhat as well as
your estimate of var(Dhat).)

- Autocorrelation, where individual animals are more or less likely to be
detected on one trip because of what has happened on previous trips. In
your case it seems plausible that the outward trip and return trip may be
correlated - either due to animals remaining in the general area over the
duration, or due to learned attraction / repulsion from the boat?

Dealing with either of those scenarios might take a bit more care.
Others may have better suggestions, but it might be worth considering
(outward + return) as a single transect/trip, depending on the behaviour
of your species of interest relative to the trip timings.


Rachel Fewster
